observation: Some business-name columns are stored encrypted at rest. Encrypted: sso_lobs.sls_name, sso_users.ssu_username, sso_services.ss_username / ss_server_ip / ss_server_host / ss_port (measured examples: 'qxAfNSm6UPULwhCamXOdFg==', 'ff/5iyC63//aqUrPI13Zkw=='). CORRECTION to this observation as first written: encryption is NARROW, not universal. Plaintext: sso_Sgroup.srv_group_name, sso_Ugroup.usr_group_name, sso_ApiUsers.Username, and the entire audit log. In every table the primary key, created_by/modified_by and created_on/modified_on are plaintext.
impact: Affects three table families rather than the whole schema. A lookup by plaintext business name fails on those tables specifically, but the plaintext audit log and the plaintext identity/timestamp columns route around it entirely - so DB validation remains viable.
workaround: Validate by integer primary key, which is always plaintext. DbPersistenceValidator.recordExistsById does this; recordExistsByName detects ciphertext in the column and reports INCONCLUSIVE rather than a false negative. For the three encrypted families, the audit log carries the plaintext object name.
status: Mitigated in framework - severity reduced from HIGH on fuller measurement
evidence: Encryption survey across key tables, tools/obj007_encryption_survey.ps1; docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md
raised_by: OBJ-007 session, corrected within the same session

observation: The at-rest encryption is deterministic - the same plaintext yields the same ciphertext everywhere, one key, no IV. sso_services holds 20,651 rows but only 59 distinct ss_port ciphertexts, with one value covering 18,848 rows (91%). The ciphertext '4QVsqJbF6MWeAvmlLMC+Kg==' appears in 3 columns across 2 tables. This is functionally AES-ECB.
impact: A security defect in a privileged-access product: deterministic encryption leaks equality and frequency, so an attacker with read access can infer plaintext by frequency analysis without any key. 59 distinct values across 20,651 rows makes the port column effectively readable.
workaround: None test-side. Ironically this is also what makes ciphertext-equality lookups work for validation, so a correct fix (randomised IV per row) will break that technique - validate by primary key instead so the test suite does not depend on the defect.

observation: sso_ApiUsers stores passwords in cleartext (observed pair AUTO40PC47 / <REDACTED>, alongside UsersSecret and UsersKey), and tbl_KeyEncryptionDecryption holds an unencrypted private key in the same database the key protects.
impact: Anyone with read access to the QA database - which now includes this automation - can read API credentials directly, and can obtain the private key needed to decrypt everything else in the same database. The key being co-located with the data it protects removes the benefit of encrypting the data at all.
workaround: None test-side. Reported for immediate escalation. This also raises the stakes on the sysadmin credential issue (OBS-013): read access to this database is read access to credentials.

observation: 16,560 of 313,197 rows in ssR_Users_Services (5.3%) reference services that no longer exist. Deletion does not cascade, and only 5 foreign keys exist across 552 tables.
impact: Dangling authorisation rows in a privileged-access-management product. Rows that grant a user access to a service persist after the service is deleted, and with almost no declared referential integrity the database cannot prevent this class of orphan. If a service identifier is ever reused, a stale grant could resolve against a new service.
workaround: None test-side. A data-integrity validation should be added once DB assertions are enabled, since this is exactly the class of defect L11 exists to catch.
evidence: Join count between ssR_Users_Services and sso_services; docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md

observation: The audit log over-reports creates by roughly 6 to 1 - six 'Created' audit rows for one actual business row.
impact: The database-side mirror of the Success:true / 'Already Exists' trap: an audit entry is not evidence of a write either. A create assertion must therefore be two-part - the audit row AND the business row - or it will confirm creates that did not happen.
workaround: DbPersistenceValidator checks business tables by primary key rather than audit rows. Any audit-based assertion must be paired with a business-table check.
status: Open - documented; framework design avoids the trap

observation: A CallBack background loop logs errors at a flat rate of about 240 per hour, continuously, before during and after any test activity. It inflated the run window's apparent error count from 194 to 1,736.
impact: Nine tenths of the errors in the run window were not test-caused. Any error-rate metric taken from this environment without excluding the CallBack loop is wrong by roughly an order of magnitude - and would have been misattributed to the test run.
workaround: Exclude the CallBack loop by predicate when measuring error rates. Fix the loop itself - it is a product defect independent of testing.
evidence: Constant-rate error counts measured before, during and after the run window; docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md

observation: Only 2 of the 6 object creations in the 2026-07-29 run window were attributable to the test - the environment has concurrent activity. A bare COUNT(*) delta across a test window is therefore unsafe.
impact: Any DB assertion built on counting rows before and after will produce false positives from other users' activity. Every count needs an attribution predicate (created_by = 'SYSTEM_API', the runner IP, or the API user id).
workaround: DbPersistenceValidator asserts on a specific primary key returned by the API rather than on counts, which sidesteps this entirely. Where a count is unavoidable, add an attribution predicate.

observation: AutoConfigs read the DB configuration from property keys that exist in no environment file: db_name read 'databaseName' and db_user_name read 'db_user', while the environment files declared db_name and db_user_name.
impact: Both fields resolved to null even in a fully populated environment, so a DB connection could never have been opened. This is the mechanical reason no DB assertion has ever run in this framework.
workaround: None needed - fixed. AutoConfigs.dbProperty() now reads the canonical key and falls back to the historic one, so environment files written against either spelling work. Upstream had independently populated QA_MsSQL.properties using the historic spellings, which the fallback covers.

observation: AutoConfigs.db_type was the hardcoded literal "mysql" while DBUtils built a jdbc:sqlserver URL and logged 'Connecting to MSSQL'. Three different databases were described in one code path.
impact: Any logic branching on db_type would have taken the MySQL path against a SQL Server target. The pom still declares mysql-connector-j 9.0.0 alongside mssql-jdbc 12.8.0.
workaround: None needed - fixed. db_type is now read from the environment and defaults to mssql.

observation: DBUtils had zero callers anywhere in the framework, and every method returned void or printed to System.out. executQuerry returned a ResultSet over a connection that getConnection() had already opened separately and getOtp then closed, so a caller could not have consumed the rows even if one existed.
impact: No test in the framework performed any database validation. The utility was unusable for assertion, not merely unused.
workaround: None needed - rewritten. query() returns fully materialised rows and closes the connection before returning; count(), exists(), queryScalar() and queryFirstRow() are assertion-shaped.
evidence: Grep for DBUtils across src/ returned only its own declaration and its main method

observation: The bearer token committed into Environments/QA_MsSQL.properties as ApiToken expired 2026-07-31 10:39 UTC (JWT nbf 2026-07-30 10:39, exp 2026-07-31 10:39 - a 24-hour token).
impact: Any suite relying on the committed token authenticates as nobody. Combined with the locked GenericScheduler account, there is no self-service path to a working token.
workaround: Owner supplies a fresh token via $env:PAM_API_TOKEN per run. Never retry /arcontoken - the account locks harder.

observation: POST /arcontoken returns HTTP 400 {"error":"Your account has been locked. Please contact your supervisor"}. The locked GenericScheduler account is also the data-warehouse ETL service account.
impact: The lockout reaches past testing into the ETL pipeline. A single shared service account for both automation and ETL means a test-side lockout is a production-side outage.
workaround: Manually issued token, one per run. Longer term the automation needs its own dedicated, non-shared service account.

observation: GET /api/ActivityLogs/GetErrorLogs and GET /api/ActivityLogs/GetLogs each hang for 30 s and stop the IIS application pool. Three sequential requests took the whole API to HTTP 503 with no recovery without intervention. This was not a load test.
impact: Three ordinary requests constitute a denial of service against the entire API surface. LH-08 puts 98 endpoints at risk.
workaround: Hard blocklist enforced at planning time, before a request is built. GetAllActiveUserDetails is blocklisted for the same reason. Live re-validation is forbidden, not merely skipped.

observation: A rejected request normally returns HTTP 200 with the rejection in the response body. Five distinct response-envelope shapes were measured on this one API, and the payload documentation describes one of them.
impact: An assertion on status alone passes against a fully rejected request. An assertion written to a fixed envelope shape fails on correct responses from endpoints with a different shape - so a generic assertion cannot be written without normalisation.
workaround: New com.arcon.utils.validation.PamEnvelope normalises all observed shapes - envelope with array/object/absent Result, bare array, error form, and both field casings - behind one accessor set.
evidence: Measured 2026-07-29; root CLAUDE.md 'Four envelope shapes'; PamEnvelope.java

observation: POST /api/ServiceCreation/SetServiceDetails returns Success:true with Message:'Already Exists' when the record already exists. Nothing is inserted; both the status code and the Success flag are green.
impact: Success:true is not evidence of a write. A create assertion built on status plus flag reports a pass for an operation that wrote nothing - the framework would have counted a no-op as a successful create.
workaround: PamApiValidator.expectInserted() asserts Message semantics and explicitly fails 'Already Exists', naming the green status and flag in the failure message so the cause is unmistakable.

observation: ApiHelper hardcoded KNOWN_ERROR_CODES = {201,202,203} and failed any test whose response carried an error code outside that set. A live run captured ErrorCode '206-LC_GLD' on HTTP 200 from POST /api/Logs/GetLogDetails - a legitimate product response the assertion would have reported as a broken test.
impact: The framework could not distinguish 'unexpected error code' from 'error code nobody documented'. Because no product error-code registry exists (4 codes documented for 1,306 endpoints), that distinction is unavailable in principle, not just in practice.
workaround: New ErrorCodeRegistry matches on the numeric prefix, includes 206, and records an unknown code as an observation rather than a failure - the defect is the missing registry, not the response.

observation: A superseded copy of validateResponseErrorCode and its caller sits commented out immediately above the live definitions in ApiHelper (roughly lines 1282-1394; the live ones follow at 1397 and 1464). A grep for the method name hits the dead block first.
impact: Any reader - human or tool - reasoning about envelope validation from a grep reaches the wrong code. It has already been necessary to warn about this in the workspace guidance.
workaround: Check for a leading // before concluding anything about behaviour. The dead block should simply be deleted; git history preserves it.

observation: WITHDRAWN - this observation as first written was wrong, and is corrected here rather than deleted. It claimed 'no row newer than 2025-10-01 exists on that server, while the API run executed 2026-07-29', and inferred that the QA API might not write to the supplied database. Both parts are false for ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA. The newest timestamp there is 2026-08-03 15:29:18 (sso_services.ss_modified_on) - minutes old at the time of measurement - and row counts rose during the session. The original figure came from sampling sso_lobs.sls_created_on in OTHER databases on the same instance, then generalising to the server. That was a sampling error on my part: one column in the wrong databases is not evidence about an instance. What remains true is that tblLOBDetail holds 0 rows, and roughly 35 AD-bridging and data-warehouse tables are empty.
impact: The correction is materially good news and reverses the conclusion: the QA API's writes DO land in ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA, confirmed three independent ways - the audit log names the created objects in plaintext (AUTO40PC47, runner IP 10.10.1.242, sal_Api_user_id=2), business tables hold them stamped created_by='SYSTEM_API' (ssu_id=1457, ss_service_id=25342, sso_ApiUsers RowId=365), and ArconPamApiLog holds 194 rows from the runner across 62 methods. DB validation is therefore possible and immediately productive. See OBS-045.
workaround: Not applicable - withdrawn. Retained so the reasoning error is visible and the corrected conclusion is traceable.
status: Withdrawn - corrected by OBS-045 within the same session
evidence: Superseded by a sweep of all 177 populated tables in ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA; docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md
raised_by: OBJ-007 session, withdrawn by OBJ-007 session

observation: Database validation is POSSIBLE against ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA and the API's writes demonstrably land there. Feasibility per type: record creation possible; update possible (sal_old_value to sal_new_value in the audit log is the only true before/after pair in the schema); deletion possible with caveats (hard deletes, so assert absence plus an audit row plus a pre-captured primary key); consistency, persistence and integrity all possible. Not possible: access-control profiles, and AD-bridging / data-warehouse objects (~35 empty tables).
impact: This is the single most valuable outcome of the objective's DB item, because DB validation is now the ONLY thing that can settle what the API-side run left open - for 101 of 107 read-backs the API evidence cannot separate 'never created' from 'created but not readable back'.
workaround: One blocker before switching it on: the configured login is sysadmin (OBS-013). Least-privilege DDL is provided in docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md section 6.1.
status: Delivered - approach documented, blocked on the account change
evidence: docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md section 1 (verdict) and section 7 (embeddable SQL per validation type); data/analysis/db-schema-map.json

observation: The database independently corroborates the API-side root-cause split. Sweeping all 177 populated tables carrying a creation timestamp, the entire 3h20m run window gained only 110 rows - 94 of them logging side-effects and roughly 7 genuine business objects.
impact: Exactly what 'most creates never happened' predicts (117 of 196 creates genuinely failed). Two independent methods - API response analysis and a full-schema database sweep - reach the same conclusion, which is the strongest form of evidence available here and makes the finding safe to escalate.
workaround: Not applicable - this is corroboration, not a defect.
evidence: 177-table creation-timestamp sweep over the run window; docs/analysis/C-database-validation.md

observation: The supplied devops login is sysadmin and dbcreator on a server hosting 30 databases, several of which are not QA (ARCOSDB, MOF_Dwh_Raw, ARCOSRDPDB_icici, OnboardingDB).
impact: An automated suite holding sysadmin over non-QA data is an unbounded blast radius. A single mistaken statement is unrecoverable, and the credential is committed in plaintext into the environment file.
workaround: Read-only discipline is enforced in code: DBUtils refuses any non-SELECT statement unless allowMutations() is called explicitly, and requests connection-level read-only from the driver (accepted by the SQL Server driver, verified). A least-privilege account scoped to the QA database with SELECT only should replace it.
status: Mitigated in framework - account change recommended

observation: System JAVA_HOME points at C:\Program Files\Java\jdk-26.0.1, which does not exist, and the java on PATH is 26.x while pom.xml requires Java 21. Maven fails until JAVA_HOME is overridden per session.
impact: Every session begins with a build that cannot run. New joiners hit it before doing any work.
workaround: $env:JAVA_HOME = 'C:\Program Files\Eclipse Adoptium\jdk-21.0.11.10-hotspot' before any mvn invocation. mvn resolves on the PowerShell PATH only, not in Bash.
evidence: Verified this session; compile succeeds only with the override

observation: APIExcelReportUtil increments a static int rowIndex with no synchronisation while API suites run parallel='classes'. ApiHelper additionally calls Playwright.create() per request and never closes the instances.
impact: Rows can overwrite each other in Api_Report.xlsx, and at 1,300+ requests the unclosed Playwright instances are a real resource leak. Both are latent at today's test counts and bite exactly when the suite is scaled to the full endpoint catalogue - which is what this objective's negative matrix implies.
workaround: None applied this session - out of scope for OBJ-007's stated items. Must be fixed before executing a full-catalogue suite.

observation: Upstream committed graphify-out/ to origin/Dev, including a 748,669-line graph.json, which collided with the locally generated untracked graphify-out/ and aborted the merge.
impact: A 150 MB regenerable build artifact is now in git history, and any developer with a locally built graph cannot merge without moving it aside first.
workaround: The local graph was moved to 'Automation gitlab repo/graphify-out.local-backup-OBJ007' (outside the repo, so it creates no git noise) and the merge then fast-forwarded cleanly. graphify-out/ should be gitignored and the committed copy removed.
evidence: git merge origin/Dev abort message; git diff --stat HEAD origin/Dev

observation: ApiHelper.validateResponseErrorCode read node.has("success") in camelCase, and Jackson is case-sensitive. A census of all 1,868 captured responses found lowercase 'success' in 0 of them and PascalCase 'Success' in 1,580. The same applied to errorCode, errorMessage, message and data.
impact: The framework's only application-envelope assertion could never pass. Every negative case that reached it failed with 'Response body missing success field' - a wrong reason, meaning the layer had zero real coverage while appearing to exist. Any green run predating this fix proves nothing about envelope behaviour.
workaround: None needed - fixed. Field access now delegates to PamEnvelope, which resolves either casing, unwraps a single-element array only when it genuinely is an envelope, and classifies the shape.
evidence: Empirical field-name census over artifacts/runs/2026-07-29_181439/evidence (1,868 files); ApiHelper.java:1533

observation: 31 distinct top-level response shapes were measured across the 1,868 captured calls. Only 6 match a documented shape; 25 do not. 127 calls are not JSON objects at all, 288 carry no Success field, 139 of 1,291 Result values are not arrays, 2 bodies are a naked true/false, and 291 lack the Program/Version/DateTime frame.
impact: Far worse than the 4-5 shapes previously recorded. No generic assertion can be written against this API without a normalisation layer, and no consumer can write a single deserialisation model.
workaround: PamEnvelope classifies into 8 shape classes, all 8 of which occur in the evidence. Root CLAUDE.md corrected from 'four envelope shapes' to the measured 31.

observation: 70 instances were measured where Success:true accompanied no write. Breakdown: 6 'Already Exists', 4 success-carrying-a-validation-error, 1 bare false, 48 success-with-no-data, 11 silent writes. The 'Already Exists' string itself varies ('Already Exists' vs 'Record Already Exists.') and appears on UserDetails/SetUserDetails and UserDetailsV3/SetUserDetails.
impact: The framework catches 0 of the 70. The harness's L1-L7 caught 14, so 56 passed every layer that ran. Any create assertion built on status plus flag is unsound, and because the message text varies, classification must be pattern-based rather than a literal match or a per-endpoint allowlist.
workaround: PamApiValidator.expectInserted() matches on message semantics with substring patterns ('insert' present and 'already exist' absent) rather than exact strings.

observation: APIConfig.java yields 1,308 distinct Controller/Action pairs against the canonical 1,306. The two extras are AzureKeyVault/GetDatabaseStatus - a real endpoint dropped from the count by a double-slash typo at APIConfig.java:188 - and User/, the SCIM root declared three times.
impact: A real endpoint is silently uncounted and therefore untested. The canonical 1,306 remains correct to quote, but the catalogue itself carries two defects.
workaround: Not corrected this session - changing the count would invalidate cross-references in every existing report. Fix the typo and the count together, deliberately.

observation: Three independent wiring gaps: 7 data providers point at Excel tables that do not exist (UAG*, UserDiscovery, Kotak) so those tests cannot run at all; 9 of 79 positive test classes are referenced by no suite XML; and 210 endpoints present in the positive Excel are absent from APIConfig.java, mostly the SCIM Service/* and User/* surface.
impact: Tests that appear to exist cannot execute, classes that exist are never scheduled, and a 210-endpoint slice of the surface is driven from Excel without a catalogue entry. Coverage counted from any single source is wrong.
workaround: None applied - reported for the owner to triage. Each is small and independently fixable.
evidence: Cross-reference of dataprovider tables, suite XMLs and APIConfig.java against the positive Excel

observation: 97 of the 107 L6 read-back checks could not have passed under any circumstances. chain_runner.store() refuses a None, so NEW_ID never entered vars; substitute() then returned the placeholder token unchanged (chain_runner.py:200); and value_anywhere() guards only against '' and 'none' (chain_runner.py:529). The check therefore deep-searched each response for the literal string '${NEW_ID}'.
impact: The headline '105 of 107 read-backs failed' is largely a harness artifact, not product evidence. Those 97 verdicts carry no information about persistence at all. Reporting them as product failures would have been wrong, and any escalation built on that number would have been indefensible.
workaround: Harness fix required in chain_runner.py: skip the L6 check when the placeholder is unresolved and record NOT RUN rather than FAIL. The framework equivalent is already correct - ValidationOutcome distinguishes NOT_RUN from FAIL precisely so this class of error cannot recur.
status: Open - harness fix outstanding; framework already models it correctly

observation: Of the 10 L6 checks that searched for a real value, 2 verified, 2 are harness false negatives (the read-back answered 'Record Already Exists.' - positive evidence of existence, recorded as FAIL), 4 never queried the store because the read-back was itself rejected with 103-ADB-SGL, and 2 genuinely returned zero rows. Two of the four extracted identifiers were not identifiers at all: an email address taken from EmailID, and a request echo of ServerDetailID: 53.
impact: For 101 of 107 hops the run cannot separate 'never created' from 'created but not readable back' - the distinguishing observation was never made. Only a read-only SELECT against ARCOSDB_U16SP2_WEBSM_QA can settle it, which is exactly what makes the DB write-target question (OBS-012) blocking rather than incidental.
workaround: Treat the L6 figures as inconclusive pending DB confirmation. Tighten identifier extraction to reject non-identifier field types.

observation: Root-cause split of the 196 MISSING ['NEW_ID'] chaining failures: 117 the create genuinely failed and no identifier ever existed (26 non-200, 89 HTTP 200 with Success:false, 2 non-standard error payloads); 19 the create was acknowledged but the response carries no identifier - a product contract gap; 0 where an identifier was present and the extractor missed it; 60 where there is neither an identifier nor a determinate create signal.
impact: The harness is not at fault - cause (c) is zero, evidenced by two searches far wider than the extractor (every dict to 12 levels, and any key matching id|code|key|guid|ref|no|num|seq|sr) finding zero hits across all 196 responses. Widening the extractor would recover none of them. The 19 acknowledged-but-no-identifier cases are a genuine API design defect: a create that returns no handle to what it created cannot be chained by anyone, including a real client.
workaround: None available test-side. The 19 need the API to return the created identifier; the 117 need valid request bodies (OBS-017).

observation: A second typo in APIConfig.java: 'Se0rviceDetailsV3' (a zero for an 'e'), which produces a hard 404 at runtime. This is distinct from the double-slash typo at APIConfig.java:188 recorded in OBS-021.
impact: A declared endpoint constant can never resolve, so whatever it was meant to cover is untested and the failure looks like a product 404 rather than a catalogue error.
workaround: Both catalogue typos should be corrected together, deliberately, since fixing them changes the canonical endpoint count that existing reports cross-reference.
evidence: APIConfig.java; observed as a 404 during the 2026-07-29 run

observation: Only 2 of 326 flows achieved a real multi-hop chain - user_lifecycle and service_lifecycle - and both were hand-written with pinned extract selectors. The depth cliff is at hop 4 to hop 5: 131 flows (40%) died at the create hop. Cumulative reach: hop 1 = 326 flows, hops 2-4 = 318, hop 5 = 187, hop 6+ = 71.
impact: Auto-generated chaining does not currently work beyond the create boundary. The two successes prove the mechanism is sound when the create returns a usable identifier - so the blocker is the API contract and the payload gap, not the generator design.
workaround: Hand-pin extract selectors for high-value lifecycles as an interim measure, which is what the two working flows do.

observation: 199 of the 279 @DataProvider names referenced by the 386 negative test classes do not exist, so 650 @Test methods fail at TestNG initialisation. Of the 80 providers that do resolve, all read the POSITIVE sheets - so for example MissingParameter/User.java runs valid data.
impact: The negative test suite is largely non-functional, and the part that does run tests the opposite of what its name claims. A test called MissingParameter that submits a complete valid payload will pass while asserting nothing about missing parameters. This is worse than absent coverage because it reads as coverage.
workaround: None applied - the scale of rewiring is beyond this objective's stated items and needs owner triage. Every negative class must be re-pointed at negative data before any negative figure from this suite can be trusted.
evidence: Cross-reference of @DataProvider names in src/test/java/com/arcon/tests/API/Negative_API/ against declared providers; docs/analysis/A3-negative-validation.md

observation: The 3,652-row negative Excel workbook is loaded by nothing. AutoConfigs.java:37 declares Negative_API_ExcelDataProviderFileName and 6 environment files set it, but no data provider reads it. 3,049 rows are unreachable, and the rows that are reachable only ever assert 405 or 401 - 2 of the 19 industry-standard negative categories.
impact: Substantial authored test data has never executed. The declared-but-unread property gives every appearance of being wired up, which is why this went unnoticed.
workaround: None applied. Either wire a provider to the negative workbook or remove the property and the workbook, but do not leave it declared and unread.
evidence: AutoConfigs.java:37; 6 environment property files; no matching reader in dataprovider/

observation: Of 10,448 generated negative scenarios across all 1,306 endpoints, 7,664 (73.4%) have no documented expected outcome at all. Only 172 (1.6%) carry a measured expected outcome; 2,612 (25%) can rely on a framework-asserted 401/405. Separately, 1,289 of 1,306 endpoints (98.7%) have zero runnable negative coverage today - only 17 endpoints across 5 of 70 controllers have any.
impact: Three quarters of a complete negative test design cannot be asserted, because nobody has documented what a rejection should look like. This quantifies precisely what the missing contract costs: the tests can be designed but not judged.
workaround: Rows are marked 'UNKNOWN - contract undocumented' rather than given a plausible guess, so the gap is countable and can be handed to development as a specific list.

observation: The endpoint count reconciles exactly, and the origin of the stale figures is now established: APIConfig.java holds 1,322 raw route constants; removing 13 surplus (11 paths declared by more than one constant) gives 1,309 distinct paths; removing 3 non-endpoints (the double-slash typo, /api/Lob/Get/{id}, /api/User) gives 1,306.
impact: Settles a recurring source of confusion. 1,322 is the raw constant count and 1,306 is the endpoint count - both are correct answers to different questions, which is why both circulated.
workaround: Quote 1,306 for endpoints and say 'route constants' when quoting 1,322. Recorded here so the distinction is not lost again.

observation: Independent confirmation of LH-08 by catalogue counting: GetLogs plus GetErrorLogs appear across exactly 98 endpoints. The full execution blocklist is 110 endpoints marked DO NOT EXECUTE - takes API down (14 named explicitly plus 96 sharing the same action name), and a further 50 endpoints marked DO NOT EXECUTE - mutating by name.
impact: Confirms the 98-endpoint figure from an entirely independent method. 160 endpoints (12% of the surface) cannot be safely executed by automation as the product currently stands.
workaround: Blocklist enforced at planning time. Guard on endpoint names, never verbs - deletion is POST /api/<Controller>/Delete<Thing>.

observation: The new validation layer is verified against real captured responses rather than invented fixtures. PamValidationLayerTest runs 15 tests over bodies taken from artifacts/runs/2026-07-29_181439/evidence, covering all 8 PamEnvelope shape classes, the Already Exists false-success trap in both measured wordings, rejection at HTTP 200, the MISSING ['NEW_ID'] failure mode, bare arrays, non-JSON bodies and leaked internals. All 15 pass.
impact: Gives the framework change evidential standing: it demonstrably handles the shapes this API actually produces, and it makes no network or database calls, so it runs anywhere without a token and cannot trip the blocklist.
workaround: Not applicable - this is the verification, not a defect.

observation: The 3-of-6,738 claim reproduces exactly (6,866 .cs files, 6,738 auto-properties, 3 [Required], 0.0445%), but the denominator is the wrong population. All three [Required] attributes sit on one class - ProvisioningService/.../Entity.cs class Request (targetHostType, rootUser, rootpass) - and there is no Provisioning* controller among the 70 under test. Those three names appear in 0 of 5,940 properties mapped to an endpoint.
impact: On the API surface actually under test the declared-required count is 0 of 5,175, not 3 of 6,738. The finding is therefore stronger than stated, not weaker: there is no declared mandatory-field metadata at all for anything being tested.
workaround: Quote both figures with their scope attached. Corroborated from a third direction: 102 of 102 archived Swagger-validated operations record 'schema declares no required properties'.

observation: Twelve constraint families return zero occurrences across pam/PAM, including all of [StringLength], [MaxLength], [MinLength], [Range], [RegularExpression] and Newtonsoft's Required = Required.Always. Yet the server demonstrably runs Newtonsoft's required check - 123 rejections of exactly that form were observed live.
impact: Decisive evidence that the models enforcing validation are not in the repository supplied. The absence of the attributes is not evidence that validation does not exist; it is evidence that the code implementing it was not provided. That reframes the developer-repo gap from 'incomplete' to 'the wrong repository'.
workaround: None test-side. Development must identify where the enforcing request models live.
evidence: docs/analysis/A5-mandatory-field-analysis.md; 123 live Newtonsoft-form rejections in the run evidence

observation: 185 of 217 create endpoints (85.3%) have no mandatory-field signal of any kind, and 66 have no known properties at all. Only 32 (14.7%) have any metadata, and 29 of those were recovered from rejection prose rather than a contract. 0 of 1,245 create body properties carry a max-length, format or pattern. The only real source is error prose - 126 endpoints, 37 field names, 5 grammars, 41 distinct messages - and the names are not canonical (UserId/UserID/UsrId, LOBId/LOBID, ServiceId/ServiceID/Service_ID).
impact: A create payload cannot be constructed from any documented source for 85% of create endpoints. Worse, the metadata gap also removes the means of diagnosis: of 213 creates called, the server named a missing property in 31 cases and stated no cause in 150.
workaround: Rejection-prose mining recovered metadata for 29 endpoints - a genuine but fragile source, since the grammar and field naming both vary.

observation: The endpoint blocklist is enforced in the documentation and in the Python harness but NOT in the Java framework's test data. testdata/API_Automation_Test_Input_Data.xls sheet AllApiPositiveScenarios contains 102 rows across 50 controllers targeting blocklisted action names - GetLogs 49, GetErrorLogs 49, GetAllActiveUserDetails 4 - every one with ExpectedStatus 200. Rows 16 and 17 are /api/ActivityLogs/GetLogs and /api/ActivityLogs/GetErrorLogs, the exact two endpoints measured to stop the IIS application pool. ActivityLogs is the single API class activated by CICD_Suites/APISuite.xml:12 and by the newly git-tracked root testng.xml.
impact: CRITICAL and live. Running the CI API suite - or opening the project in an IDE, which picks up a root testng.xml by convention - drives the two endpoints that took the whole API to HTTP 503 after three sequential calls with no self-recovery. The safety rule that has governed every manual and harness run since it was discovered has no equivalent inside the framework the CI pipeline actually executes. It is protected today only by the fact that nobody has run that suite.
workaround: Not applied - a framework change is outside OBJ-008's stated scope and OBJ-007's work is still uncommitted awaiting review, so adding more would muddy that review. Recommended fix is a name-based guard in ApiHelper that refuses a request whose action name is blocklisted, failing the test with a clear message rather than issuing the call - guarding on names, never verbs. Removing the 102 rows is the alternative but is fragile, since nothing then stops them being re-added.
status: Open - reported, awaiting a decision on the guard
evidence: xlrd scan of testdata/API_Automation_Test_Input_Data.xls sheet AllApiPositiveScenarios (1,865 rows); CICD_Suites/APISuite.xml:12; root testng.xml; ISSUE-010 for the app-pool capture; LH-08

observation: A root testng.xml now exists and is git-tracked, having arrived in the upstream Dev merge (commit 4a40b81). It runs one class - ActivityLogs - and carries no <listeners> block. Both AGENTS.md section TestNG suites and the repo CLAUDE.md section Commands still assert 'There is no root testng.xml'.
impact: Two consequences. IDEs pick up a root testng.xml by convention, so this is a plausible accidental route into OBS-047 - a developer pressing Run on the project could drive the app-pool-killing endpoints without ever opening a suite file. And with no listeners registered, TestListener never runs, so APIExcelReportUtil is never initialised and no Excel report is produced - the same trap as -Dtest.
workaround: Correct both documents. Either delete the root testng.xml or give it listeners and a safe class; leaving an undocumented, listener-less root suite pointing at the most dangerous class in the catalogue is the worst of the options.

observation: Mandatory-field metadata is effectively unavailable: 3 properties of roughly 6,738 carry a Required marker, and there is no length, format or pattern validation metadata anywhere in the supplied sources.
impact: A generated create payload cannot be known-valid, so a create cannot be reliably driven; a failed create returns no identifier; without an identifier a chain cannot proceed past its first hop. It also makes an honest 'missing mandatory field' negative test impossible to author, because which field is mandatory is unknown.
workaround: PamApiValidator records L9_MANDATORY_FIELDS as NOT_RUN with an explicit reason when no mandatory set is supplied, so the gap is visible in every report instead of being absorbed as a pass.
